opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think one thing people often get wrong is assuming that once AI can do a job, it'll immediately be deployed to do that job everywhere. But compute is a finite resource, at least in the short-to-medium term, and as AI systems get more capable, the value you can extract from a given unit of compute goes up. So there's going to be real competition over where that compute gets allocated.

What that implies is that automation will roughly follow where the marginal value of compute is highest, not just where AI is technically capable. If you have an AI system that can do both, say, customer service and frontier AI research, and running it on AI research is worth vastly more per GPU-hour, then a lot of the compute gets pulled toward the high-value stuff. In the world I worry most about, the single highest-value use is probably accelerating AI R&D itself, because that compounds. So you might see AI companies dedicating huge fractions of their compute to automating their own research, while lots of ordinary jobs that are technically automatable stay done by humans for a while, simply because the opportunity cost of the compute is too high.

Over time that changes. Compute keeps scaling, algorithms get more efficient, inference gets cheaper, and the frontier of "worth automating" sweeps outward into more and more of the economy. But it could be pretty uneven. You might get this weird period where AI is doing an enormous amount of cognitive work inside a few labs, and from the outside the broader labor market looks surprisingly normal, maybe with some disruption in the obviously cheap-to-automate stuff like certain kinds of writing, coding, and support work.

I think that's important for a few reasons. One, it means labor market statistics might be a lagging and misleading indicator of how far AI has actually gotten. Two, it concentrates a lot of capability and economic leverage in whoever controls the compute. And three, from a safety perspective, the most intense, least-supervised deployment might happen exactly in the place that matters most: AI systems doing AI research, potentially with large amounts of autonomy, before society at large has really noticed things have changed.

So I'd say competition for compute probably delays broad job automation relative to what pure capability would suggest, but it doesn't delay the transformative stuff. It might actually focus it.

r001.rationale: The response says compute will go to uses with the highest marginal value and gives AI research as an example, but it does not suggest that the highest-wage jobs will be automated first.

r002.rationale: It says AI companies may dedicate huge fractions of compute to automating their own research because AI R&D is likely the highest-value use.

r003.rationale: The response suggests compute competition could delay broad job automation, but does not raise the possibility that existing automation trends could reverse.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underrated dynamics in how automation plays out, and it cuts against the simplest story people tell.

The naive story is: once AI can do a job, the job gets automated. But that ignores that running AI isn't free. Every token of inference is compute, and compute is going to be scarce for a while, probably more scarce than people expect. So the real question isn't "can the AI do this task?" It's "is this task the most valuable thing you could be doing with that compute?"

And I think the answer, for a lot of ordinary jobs, is going to be no, at least in the early period. If you're a frontier lab, or really anyone with access to a lot of compute, the highest value use is probably AI research itself, or other things that feed back into making the AI better or into high-stakes strategic stuff. Automating a mid-level accounting job might be totally feasible, but if the marginal GPU could instead be doing something that accelerates your capabilities by some fraction of a percent, you're going to point it there. So you get this weird situation where the capability to automate a job exists well before the economic pressure to actually do it.

The other piece is that this makes the automation curve really lumpy in a way that's hard to predict. The jobs that get automated first won't necessarily be the ones AI is best at. They'll be the ones where the value per unit of compute is highest relative to what else the compute could be doing. That's partly about how much the human costs, but also about how much inference you need per unit of output. Something like software engineering where you might need a lot of tokens of reasoning and iteration per task is actually compute-expensive, whereas some lower-skill jobs might need very little. So you could end up with a pattern that looks pretty strange from the outside.

And then there's a phase change to worry about. At some point, if we do get something like full automation of AI R&D, the amount of effective compute available grows really fast, and the constraint relaxes. Then you'd expect automation to hit a huge range of jobs almost all at once, rather than gradually. So my overall picture is: slower than capabilities alone would suggest at first, driven by compute allocation rather than capability, and then potentially very abrupt. I'd put a lot of weight on that abruptness being the thing that actually matters for how society handles it.

I should flag I'm uncertain about the magnitudes here. If compute gets cheap faster than I think, or if labs don't actually have that many high-value internal uses, the gradual phase could be much shorter. But the basic point that compute competition, not capability, is the binding constraint seems pretty robust to me.

r001.rationale: The response says automation depends on value per unit of compute and notes that human cost is one factor, but it does not suggest the highest-wage jobs will be automated first.

r002.rationale: It says AI research is probably the highest-value use of compute and could take priority over automating ordinary jobs, even when the AI can perform them.

r003.rationale: The response describes automation being delayed and uneven because compute has competing uses, but does not raise a possible reversal of existing job-automation trends.

astra-6.text:
I think a key question is what else you could be doing with the compute. It’s not enough for an AI to be capable of doing your job. It has to be worth allocating compute to that task, relative to all the other tasks that compute could be doing.

So, for example, suppose AI systems can automate a lot of remote work, but they’re also extremely useful for AI research. You could end up with a situation where a substantial fraction of the available compute goes toward developing better AI systems, because that has a higher return than automating some relatively low-paid job. That job might remain economically viable for humans even though AI could technically do it.

There’s a countervailing force, which is that you can build more compute and make the systems more efficient. And a model that’s sufficient for some ordinary task might be much cheaper to run than the system you use for cutting-edge research. So I wouldn’t infer that competition for compute necessarily delays automation by a very long time.

But it does mean that capability alone doesn’t tell you the order or speed of automation. You also need to know how much compute each task takes, how valuable it is, and how quickly the supply of compute can expand.

r001.rationale: The response says compute may go to tasks with higher returns than automating relatively low-paid jobs, but it does not suggest that the highest-wage jobs would be automated first.

r002.rationale: It gives AI research as a competing use that may receive substantial compute, but does not say it gets most automation attention when AI is most capable of automating work.

r003.rationale: It notes that competing compute uses can make some jobs remain viable for humans, but does not raise the possibility that existing automation trends could reverse.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one thing people sometimes miss is that being able to automate a job doesn’t necessarily mean it’s immediately worth automating. You also have to ask what else you could do with the compute.

Suppose you have an AI that can do some administrative task more cheaply than a human at current compute prices. If that same compute can be used to do extremely valuable research, or to improve the next generation of AI systems, then demand for those uses could push the price up. And at that higher price, employing the human might still make sense.

So you could get a period where AI is technically capable of doing a very wide range of jobs, but deployment is concentrated in the activities where it generates the most value per unit of compute. That could produce a fairly strange pattern of automation, where some difficult, highly paid work gets automated while some easier work continues to be done by humans.

Of course, the supply of compute can expand, and systems can become more efficient. So this isn’t necessarily a durable protection for human employment. It’s more a reason to distinguish between when AI can do a task and when allocating compute to that task makes economic sense.

r001.rationale: It says highly paid work may be automated while easier work remains human-performed because compute goes to higher-value uses, conveying that high-wage jobs could be automated first.

r002.rationale: It mentions research and improving future AI as valuable competing uses of compute, but does not say AI R&D may receive most automation attention when AI is most capable of automating work.

r003.rationale: It says compute competition could make human labor economically preferable in some tasks, but does not raise the possibility that existing automation trends could reverse because inference compute outbids those applications.
